title: Low-precision burst profiling and failure catalog
content:
Overview

This is a working note that documents a focused set of experiments and observed failure modes when running low-precision (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ) variants under short-duration, high-concurrency bursts. The goal: identify reproducible "fracture points" where latency, tail behavior, or quality regressions appear nonlinearly during bursts vs steady-state.

Why this matters (motivation)
- Many production workloads are bursty (search spikes, chat surges). Quantized kernels are tuned for average throughput, but we have observed non-obvious regressions under short bursts: tail latency spikes, KV cache thrash, kernel misspeculation timeouts, and sporadic quality drops.
- We need a compact, repeatable failure catalog so rollout playbooks can map observed symptoms -> mitigations (fallback policy, throttling, kernel pinning, temporary mix-precision).

Scope and definitions
- "Burst": short window (1s-30s) where QPS ramps to 5–20x baseline.
- "Fracture point": parameter combination (bitwidth, kernel, batchshape, hw) where a burst produces a severe degradation (latency > 3x p95, >10% quality regression, or error rate spike).
- HW used here: A100-80GB and H100-80GB across linux instances used by CI cluster.
- Models: family-agnostic tests on Open7B-like and Open13B-like checkpoints compiled to our runtime variants.

Hypotheses we want to verify
1) Short bursts exacerbate kernel scheduling jitter, causing latency amplification when using mixed-precision kernels with large KV footprints.
2) AWQ/GPTQ low-bit kernels are more sensitive to batchshape variability during bursts due to packing inefficiencies.
3) FP8 kernels show fewer quality regressions under burst but sometimes higher memory pressure causing eviction cascades.
4) Prefix-caching (KV cache) thrash during bursts causes disproportionate compute-to-memory stalls on certain kernel implementations.

Test harness (what we run)
- Load generator: internal harness that simulates realistic prompt-length distribution and user think-times; configurable ramp/hold/drop profiles.
- Sequence lengths: 64, 256, 1024, 2048 (where applicable).
- Concurrency targets: baseline (1x), medium (3–5x), burst (10–20x).
- Batch shaping: fixed-batch (pad to max), dynamic-batch (pack by length), zero-padding (no packing).
- Kernels: our set of optimized kernels described internally as lane-compact, block-packed, and stream-kv (note: these map to internal kernel flavors; avoid exposing micro impl details here).
- Quantization variants: INT8 (per-channel symmetric/asymmetric), FP8 (e4m3 and e5m2 formats), GPTQ (per-tensor fine-tuned), AWQ (activation-aware per-block).
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency, error rate (failed responses), memory high-water mark, KV cache eviction rate, top-of-stack kernel retry counts, and quality deltas (BLEU/ROUGE proxies where applicable plus a small prompt-based eval set for hallucination/regression scoring).

Experiment matrix (summary)
- For each model size (7B/13B), for each HW (A100/H100), for each quant variant (INT8, FP8-e4m3, FP8-e5m2, GPTQ, AWQ), we sweep: batchshape policy (3), seq len (4), concurrency (3). Targeted runs focused on bursts: short-ramp (1s to peak), step-ramp (instant), and sawtooth (repeated micro-bursts).

Preliminary findings (high level)
- Throughput vs latency: Some INT8 lane-compact kernels produce the best amortized throughput but show p99 spikes under instant ramp (step-ramp). The spikes correlate with kernel scheduling backpressure when batch queues fill quickly.
- Quality: AWQ and GPTQ maintain the best quality consistency across bursts. However, in one configuration AWQ experienced a 6% increase in low-confidence outputs under repeated micro-bursts at seq_len=2048 on A100.
- Memory: FP8-e5m2 shows lower nominal memory but a higher observed KV eviction rate during bursts on H100 for large sequences; eviction cascades lead to repeated recomputation and latency tail amplification.
- Kernel mismatch: stream-kv kernel (optimized for long sequences) under short-burst small sequences triggers a fallback path that has heavy synchronization and caused 2–3x p95 regression. This was not obvious until we simulated step-ramp bursts.

Failure catalog (symptoms -> likely cause -> quick mitigations)
1) Symptom: p99 spikes only during instantaneous step-ramp bursts; p50 stable.
   Likely cause: scheduling backpressure + kernel launch serialization when many small batches arrive simultaneously.
   Mitigations: enable "burst-queue" smoothing (internal flag), prefer block-packed kernel for bursts, limit instantaneous concurrency with short tokenized queueing.

2) Symptom: elevated KV eviction rate with matching p95 regression and more low-confidence outputs.
   Likely cause: FP8 memory packing interacting poorly with KV cache eviction heuristics under burst. Evicted keys cause recompute of prefixes and degrade quality via lost cached context.
   Mitigations: increase KV retention for high-priority routes temporarily during bursts, switch to an INT8 variant for the burst window, or enable partial-cache-reserve for long-seq requests.

3) Symptom: quality regression (scored eval delta >5%) under rapid repeated micro-bursts for AWQ on large seq lengths.
   Likely cause: micro batching causes packing artifacts that expose block-level quantization sensitivity (AWQ block boundaries misaligned across requests).
   Mitigations: enforce deterministic packing for critical routes, fall back to mixed-precision for a small percentage of requests, add per-route micro-burst throttle in router.

4) Symptom: rare "timeout with retry" errors correlated to kernel retry counters and temp spike in CPU-side spin loops.
   Likely cause: kernel path fallback that retries with different kernel flavor under concurrency. If fallback paths are not lock-free, we amplify CPU contention.
   Mitigations: make fallback non-blocking, reduce fallback aggressiveness during high concurrency windows, increase diagnostic sampling to capture stack traces at time of retry.

Repro recipe (how to reproduce locally)
- Check out PR branch perf/burst-profile (example harness live in the repo).
- Launch harness with: 
  * model=open7b-variant, hw=A100, quant=awq, kernel=stream-kv
  * ramp profile: step -> peak QPS 15 for 10s, hold 10s, drop
  * sequence length: 2048, packing=dynamic
- Collect: metrics/export-latency.json, kernel-retry.log, kv-evictions.csv, samples/failed-outputs.json
- Quick grep: kernel-retry.log for >50 retries, correlate with kv-evictions.csv timestamps -> you should see eviction spikes aligning with p95 jump.

Open questions and follow-ups
- How does scheduler fairness across multiple model tenants change fracture points? Do multi-tenant bursts produce new failure modes?
- Can we create an adaptive scheduler that detects micro-bursts and temporarily switches kernels/policies without user-level config?
- Is there an efficient per-route micro-cache reservation mechanism that avoids global KV eviction cascades?

Action items (next steps)
- [Priya] Automate the reproduc recipe into CI harness and add a nightly short-burst job across our two HW clouds. Target: detect regressions <24h after kernel changes.
- [Daniel] Investigate making fallback non-blocking and prototype a low-contention fallback queue.
- [María] Run a multi-tenant burst test (3 tenants with staggered peaks) and capture cross-tenant interference patterns.
- [Kenji] Add a compact telemetry histogram for per-kernel retry and eviction pairing and expose via console as a temporary diagnostic panel.

Appendix: quick notes
- Observed that step-ramp exposes more issues than sawtooth in our kernels; include both in any benchmark.
- For quality checks use the small curated eval set (internal id: burst-eval-42). Avoid large offline evals for quick runs.
- Suggest adding a "burst-mode" knob to the router to allow safe temporary policy changes during autoscaling.

Notes to self
- Keep this doc compact; split into a playbook and a reproducible test spec once the CI runs stabilize.
- We should anonymize internal kernel names if this leaks externally.

End of working note.
